title: Final forms and look-alike letters

objectives.can: Recognise the five final forms and tell apart the letters that look alike.

explanation.summary: Five letters are written differently when they end a word, and several other letters look so much like each other that beginners confuse them. This lesson teaches the five final forms and sets the look-alike letters side by side, so that you can read a word without guessing.

sections.heading: Five letters with two shapes
body: Five letters have a second shape that is used only when the letter is the last letter of a word. The name and the sound do not change. The ordinary shape is used everywhere else. A word never ends in the ordinary shape of these five letters, and never has the final shape in the middle.
Four of the final forms drop below the line of writing: ך ן ף ץ. The fifth, ם, stays on the line and is closed and square. That is a quick way to find the end of a word.

sections.heading: Both shapes in one word
body: A word may contain both shapes of the same letter. The word for 'the heavens' in the first verse of the Bible has a mem in the middle and a final mem at the end. Read it from the right and you meet the ordinary form first; the form that closes the word is the final one.

A final form belongs to the end of a word as it is printed. A word joined to the next by a short horizontal line (the maqqef, lesson H0.3.2) is still a separate printed word and still ends with its final form, as the example from Genesis 8:9 shows.

sections.heading: Letters that look alike
body: The second table sets the main look-alikes side by side. Beginners most often confuse ב and כ, ג and נ, ד and ר, ה, ח and ת, ו and ז, and ס and the final ם. Two more pairs, ט and מ, and ע and צ, differ in the details of the shape. The descriptions in the table fit the usual printed type; other fonts shift the details, so check each against real words.
The best remedy is to read real words and to look carefully at each letter. Do not guess a word from its first letters: a wrong letter often makes a different word, or none.

sections.heading: Shin and sin
body: The letter ש stands for two sounds, told apart by a small dot. With the dot over its right-hand arm it is shin (שׁ), pronounced sh. With the dot over the left-hand arm it is sin (שׂ), pronounced s. Printed Hebrew nearly always carries the dot; if there is none, you must know the word. The dots are treated again in lesson H0.2.3.

misunderstandings: A final form is not a different letter. ם is mem, and it sounds as מ does; it is only the shape that closes a word.

The ordinary shape of the five letters never stands at the end of a word. If you see כ, מ, נ, פ or צ at the left-hand end of a word, you have probably misread a letter, because the ordinary shapes do not close a word.
Look-alike letters are not interchangeable. ר for ד changes the word, and so do ה for ח and ב for כ.
The dot of shin or sin belongs to the letter, and it changes the sound. It is not a vowel.

deeper.heading: Final forms in the history of the script
body: The early Hebrew script did not use separate final forms. They belong to the square script, in which a few letters came to be written differently at the end of a word. The fixed use of the five forms is familiar from the medieval manuscripts, and Hebrew Bibles keep it.

rows: Bet has a flat base with a corner at the lower right that sticks out a little. Kaf is rounded at the bottom, without a corner.
Kaf is rounded at the bottom, without a corner. Bet has a square base.
Gimel has a slanting leg joined to its right-hand stem. Nun has a flat base that runs left from the stem, and is shorter.
Nun has a flat base that runs left from the stem. Gimel has a slanting leg.
Dalet has a square corner at the top right, where the roof overhangs. Resh has a rounded corner.
Resh has a rounded corner at the top right. Dalet has a square one.
He has a gap between its left leg and its roof. Het is closed: both legs join the roof.
Het is closed at the top, with both legs joined to the roof. He has a gap; tav has a small foot on its left leg.
Tav has a small foot on its left leg and a curved roof at the left. Het has two plain legs.
Vav is a straight stroke with a small hook at the top. Zayin has a bar across the top that overhangs on both sides.
Zayin has a bar across the top that overhangs on both sides. Vav has only a small hook.
Yod is the smallest letter, a short stroke hanging from the top of the line. Vav is a longer straight stroke.
Final nun is a long straight stroke that drops below the line; vav stays on the line and is shorter.
Tet has a rounded bowl at the bottom, curving in at the top left. Mem is angular, with a corner at the lower right.
Mem is angular and has a corner at the lower right. Tet is rounded.
Samekh is round. Final mem is closed with straight sides and square corners.
Final mem is closed with straight sides and square corners. Samekh is round.
Ayin has a stem with a V-shape at the top. Tsade has a small head at the right and a tail under it.
Tsade has a small head at the right and a tail that reaches back under it. Ayin is a V on a stem.
Shin has the dot over its right-hand arm and sounds sh.
Sin has the dot over its left-hand arm and sounds s.
paradigms.note: Check each pair against real words, because fonts differ in the details.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two words of the first verse end in a final form. The first has a mem in the middle and a final mem at the end: read from the right, you meet the ordinary form first, then the closed ם last. The second word ends in final tsade, which drops below the line; the ordinary צ would not be written here.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: This word ends in final kaf, ך, a long stroke below the line, with two small dots under it (a vowel sign taught in lesson H0.2.2). Contrast the ordinary כ, which you will meet in the middle of other words. The word's first letter is vav, the small word 'and' joined to what follows.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Both highlighted words end in the final nun, ן. It is a straight stroke below the line, and it must not be read as a vav, which stays on the line. In the second word the first letter, vav, is the small word 'and'; the rest is the same word as the first.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him to the ark, for the waters were on the face of the whole earth; and he put forth his hand, and took her, and brought her in unto him into the ark.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The highlighted word ends in final pe, ף, followed by a short joining line (maqqef) that ties it to the next word. Its ordinary form פ is the one you would see in the middle of a word.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: AND IT came to pass in the days when the judges judged, that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Beth-lehem in Judah went to sojourn in the field of Moab, he, and his wife, and his two sons.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: This word has a sin, שׂ, with its dot over the left-hand arm, so it begins with the s sound. Compare the shin, שׁ, in a later word of the same verse, וְאִשְׁתּוֹ: the letter is the same, and only the dot differs.

reading.why: Three verses with names and plain words, and many of the pairs of this lesson: final mem, final kaf, sin and shin, he and het. Read the letters aloud one by one from the right, and notice every final form.
